taxonomy.subtopic: NADPH oxidase failure and absent dihydrorhodamine fluorescence shift

questions.stem_html: A 4-year-old boy has recurrent lymph-node and pulmonary infections caused by Serratia marcescens and Aspergillus species. After neutrophils are stimulated in vitro, the accompanying flow-cytometry histogram shows no rightward shift in dihydrorhodamine fluorescence compared with the unstimulated sample. Which reaction is defective?

options.text_html: Reduction of oxygen to water in the mitochondrial electron transport chain
Transfer of electrons from NADPH to molecular oxygen to generate superoxide
Conversion of superoxide to hydrogen peroxide by superoxide dismutase
Conversion of hydrogen peroxide and chloride to hypochlorous acid by myeloperoxidase
Degradation of microbial hydrogen peroxide by catalase

questions.explanation_html: The dihydrorhodamine assay measures the phagocyte respiratory burst. In chronic granulomatous disease, defective NADPH oxidase prevents electron transfer from NADPH to oxygen and therefore prevents superoxide production. Downstream reactive oxygen species are reduced, causing impaired intracellular killing and susceptibility to catalase-positive bacteria and fungi. Stimulated neutrophils consequently fail to develop the normal fluorescence shift.

wrong_choice_explanations.2: Myeloperoxidase acts downstream of hydrogen peroxide. Its deficiency usually has a much milder phenotype and the respiratory burst measured by dihydrorhodamine is present.
wrong_choice_explanations.3: Superoxide dismutase converts superoxide to hydrogen peroxide; the initiating defect in chronic granulomatous disease occurs before superoxide is formed.
wrong_choice_explanations.4: Catalase is a microbial and host enzyme that breaks down hydrogen peroxide; its activity is not the neutrophil defect measured by this assay.
wrong_choice_explanations.5: Mitochondrial oxidative phosphorylation is not the phagocyte oxidase system responsible for the respiratory burst.

questions.educational_objective: Chronic granulomatous disease results from NADPH oxidase failure, causing absent superoxide generation and an abnormal dihydrorhodamine oxidative-burst assay.

media.alt_text: Original flow-cytometry histogram comparing the normal rightward dihydrorhodamine fluorescence shift after neutrophil stimulation with the absent shift in chronic granulomatous disease.
